items.title: 5,800 to 53,000 req/s by skipping the filter chain
items.text:
I made a Spring endpoint nine times faster this week. The way I did it is by skipping most of what Spring does to keep you safe.

A minimal echo endpoint on the standard Spring MVC path gave 5,800 requests per second. The same endpoint on my fast path gave 53,000. The numbers are from a real application with several hundred mappings, not from a hello world project.

Echo endpoint, requests per second. Higher is better. Standard Spring MVC 5,800 Fast path 53,000

So for a simple endpoint, about nine tenths of the request is spent before your code runs. The request goes through every servlet filter, the security filter chain parses the same path again for each pattern it holds, and then the DispatcherServlet finds the handler. With hundreds of mappings and a long list of security patterns, that work is far larger than an echo.
path: 5,800 to 53,000 req/s by skipping the filter chain

items.title: What the library does
items.text:
spring-mvc-fastpath is a Spring Boot starter. You mark the hot endpoints:

@MvcAccelerator
@GetMapping("/echo")
public String echo(@RequestParam String value)
{
    return value;
}

Requests to those take a short route past the DispatcherServlet, and run only the filters you list:

mvc:
  accelerator:
    fast-filter-chain:
      mode: ANNOTATED
      fail-if-filter-missing: true
      included-filters:
        - com.example.filters.MyCustomLoggingFilter

There is also a request matcher that caches the parsed path for the length of one request, so the security chain does not parse it again for every pattern. That one is safe to use by itself.
path: 5,800 to 53,000 req/s by skipping the filter chain

items.title: A shortcut around security
items.text:
I am normally the one who says no to shortcuts around security. This library is a shortcut around security, and the first thing in its README is a warning.

A filter you did not list does not run. If that filter was the one doing authentication, the endpoint is open, and nothing will tell you. That is why fail-if-filter-missing is on by default, so a typo in a class name stops the application at startup. It does not help if you forget the filter altogether.

For most endpoints it is not worth it. Once the handler does a database call, the framework overhead is a small part of the request and the gain goes away. It pays off for the few endpoints that are hit all the time and do almost nothing.

It is not in production with us. I am not sure it should be.
path: 5,800 to 53,000 req/s by skipping the filter chain

items.title: 661 backups and none of them off-site
items.text:
At work I would never accept a system without a tested, off-site backup. At home I ran one for years, and it held everything I actually care about.

I only found out because I was doing something else. I wanted the home server written down as Ansible, so I could rebuild it if it died. Before changing anything I went through what was there.

Home Assistant had 661 backups. 335 GB of them, on the same SSD as Home Assistant itself. So one dead disk would take the system and every backup of it at the same moment. The disk was also 97% full, and the backups were the reason.

It gets worse. I did have a backup script. I wrote it myself, it zipped things to that same SSD, and I never put it on a timer. I ran it by hand until I stopped, and that turned out to be January 2025.

I also had a cloud remote, rclone to Google Drive through my own OAuth app. That one is almost funny. An app left in "Testing" gets a token that expires after 7 days. So it worked for a week, and then it answered invalid_grant to nobody for a very long time.

So I had backups, a backup script and a cloud remote, and no backup.

Backup data, GB Kept on the same SSD 335 GB, 661 files Off-site set now 15 GB
path: 661 backups and none of them off-site

items.title: Why I let it happen
items.text:
None of this is hard, and that is the uncomfortable part. I know how to do it, and I do it properly for other people's data every day.

I think it is because at work somebody asks. There is a review, an audit, a colleague who wants to see the restore. At home nobody asks, and everything just keeps working, so it feels fine. Home Assistant even helps you feel fine, since it makes a backup every night and keeps all of them. 661 nights of it.

The data at home is the data I cannot get back from anyone. I treated it the worst.
path: 661 backups and none of them off-site

items.title: What I did about it
items.text:
Home Assistant now keeps 3 backups. A restic snapshot goes off-site every night at 03:30. The databases are dumped properly first, sqlite3 .backup for SQLite and --single-transaction for MySQL, since copying a live database file gives you something that only looks like a backup. I keep 14 daily, 8 weekly and 12 monthly, and every Sunday 5% of the data is read back.

The whole off-site set is about 15 GB. I had been keeping 335.

The part I care most about is small. The job reports its state to Home Assistant, and I get a notification on anything but ok. I also get one when 36 hours pass without a run. The first rule would not have saved me. My old script never failed, it just never ran, and a job that never starts sends no error.

And I still got it wrong on the first try. One path in the backup list no longer existed. restic exits with code 3 on that, my script had set -e, and so it would have stopped before pruning old snapshots, every night, quietly. That is the same mistake a third time. It was caught in review before the first run, which says something about reviews and something about me.
path: 661 backups and none of them off-site

items.title: What I still skimp on
items.text:
The camera recordings are 1.2 TB and live on the RAID only. Too big to send anywhere, I tell myself. The RAID is 83% full.

I would not accept that answer from anyone at work.
path: 661 backups and none of them off-site

items.title: A gateway that logs every body
items.text:
"We sent it correctly." I have heard that sentence many times, and most of the time I could not check it.

It happens when a new client is onboarded, and even more when it is a client's client. They integrate with us through someone else's system, and often nobody on their side knows what that system sends. We see a rejected request in our logs. We do not see what was in it.

Application logs do not help much here. They log what the application understood, and the problem is usually in the part it did not understand.

So I put a gateway in front that keeps everything. cloud-gateway is a reverse proxy built on Spring Cloud Gateway. It logs the full request and response, headers and body, to ClickHouse, and there is a Grafana dashboard on top.

docker-compose up -d
curl -uuser:pass http://localhost:6464/get

Then Grafana on port 3000 shows the traffic.

Added later: the dashboard during a test run in October 2023, with ApacheBench against httpbin.

Now the answer to "we sent it correctly" is the request itself. That ends the discussion quickly, and not always in our favour. Sometimes they did send it correctly.

I know what I am doing here. Bodies hold personal data and secrets, and a full log of them is something I would question in anyone else's design. It needs access control and a short retention time, and it should be on only where it is needed. I think it is worth it for support and remediation. I am less sure I would accept the argument from someone else.
path: A gateway that logs every body

items.title: A gateway that remembers every request
items.text:
Recording every request body costs my new gateway about a third of its throughput. I think that is cheap.

The reason is a question I have been asked too many times: what did the client actually send us?

It comes up when a new client is onboarded. It comes up more when it is a client's client, and nobody on the call knows what their system sends. Somebody says the request was correct, somebody else says it was not, and without a record it is one word against another. With a record it takes a minute.

I have had this since 2023 in cloud-gateway, built on Spring Cloud Gateway. It did the job. Two things about it wore me down.

The first is configuration. Spring accepts anything. Write foo.bar=baz and it starts without a word, so you have no idea whether a setting stuck or had any effect. A misspelled filter is found by the request that should have gone through it.

The second is the cost of recording on the request path.
path: A gateway that remembers every request

items.title: What r7 does differently
items.text:
r7 has one routes.yaml, and it is checked before a single request is served. Unknown keys, misspelled filters, bad regular expressions and missing variables stop it at startup with a message. A bad edit to a running gateway is rejected, and the old routes keep serving.

The status page, here with demo routes. The last column shows the journal level per route.

routes:
  - id: api
    match:
      - PathPrefix:
          prefix: /api
    upstream:
      targets:
        - url: http://backend:8080
    journal:
      request:
        level: FULL
      response:
        level: FULL

The journal is written to memory-mapped files on local disk, so there is no network call while the client waits. A separate process, the tailer, reads the files afterwards and ships them as JSON lines and as WARC, the format web archives use. Secret header and query values are stored as fingerprints and not as the values.
path: A gateway that remembers every request

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
It is not free, and I would not trust anyone who said it was. Measured on two cores, against the same gateway with the journal off:

Journal level Throughput lost METADATA 4 to 14% HEADERS 21 to 25% FULL 34 to 54%

Throughput lost per journal level, percent. Lowest to highest across the scenarios. METADATA 4 to 14% HEADERS 21 to 25% FULL 34 to 54% 0% 20% 40% 60%

The 54% is a browser page with 8 KB of HTML recorded on every request. For API calls, FULL costs about a third of the throughput, and adds about 1.5 ms at p99 at 20,000 requests per second.

So recording every body costs a third of the gateway. I think that is cheap for what it answers, on the routes where the question gets asked. On the rest you record headers, or nothing. It is set per route, and it can turn itself up when a response fails.
path: A gateway that remembers every request

items.title: Where it stands
items.text:
On the same two cores r7 sustains 2.3 to 2.9 times what cloud-gateway does. nginx is faster than both by a wide margin, and r7 adds about 2 ms at p99 over it. If you only need a reverse proxy, use nginx.

r7 is pre-release. It does not terminate TLS and has no scripting language, on purpose.
path: A gateway that remembers every request

items.title: A K2 firmware update deletes your config and your root
items.text:
I rooted my printer, changed its config, and then got annoyed when a firmware update did not respect my changes.

That is not a fair complaint, and I know it. The update was still sloppy.

On 17 November I updated the K2 Pro to 1.1.8.3. Afterwards the printer sat in an error state and would not print. Klipper said:

Include file printdrop.cfg does not exist

The update had reset the factory config files and deleted the one file that was mine. But it kept printer.cfg, and that file still had my line in it:

[include printdrop.cfg]

So it removed the file and kept the reference to it. Either choice alone would have been fine. Keep both and nothing breaks. Remove both and I lose my macros but the printer starts. Half of each gives a printer that halts at startup.

Root was gone too. The SSH host key had changed and my key was refused.
path: A K2 firmware update deletes your config and your root

items.title: The fix
items.text:
The Moonraker file API still works after the update, without root. So recovery is one upload of the missing file to the config folder, and then FIRMWARE_RESTART. A plain RESTART is not enough.

Klipper came back as ready, and the calibration from 1 November was still there, since it lives in printer.cfg.
path: A K2 firmware update deletes your config and your root

items.title: What I do now
items.text:
I assume every update will do the same. The config file lives in my own repo and not only on the printer, and putting it back takes a minute.

If you have added an include of your own to a K2, check that you have a copy of the file somewhere else before you press update.
path: A K2 firmware update deletes your config and your root

items.title: A Kafka-like queue on MySQL
items.text:
Everybody knows you should not build a message queue on a database. I just did, and I think it was the right call.

What I needed was small. Events have to be kept for a few days. A client that reconnects must be able to say "I have seen up to message 45,610" and get the rest. The volume is a few tens of messages per second.

Kafka does that, and it is what I would pick for real volume. But a Kafka cluster is something you operate. It needs ZooKeeper, monitoring and someone who knows what to do when a broker is unhappy. For tens of messages per second that is absurd, and we already run MySQL.

So kfka keeps the part of Kafka I needed. Messages are rows in one table, and the client holds its own offset.

One table, ordered by id. The client says what it saw last and gets the rest. 45,608 45,609 45,610 45,611 45,612 45,613 lastSeenMessageId delivered on reconnect, then live 

kfkaManager.addListener((msg) ->
{
    // handle message
},
new KfkaPredicate()
    .topic("chat")
    .lastSeenMessageId(45_610)       // next message will be 45,611
    .addPropertyMatch("userId", 123));

A new listener can also rewind, and get up to the last 100 messages before the live ones. That makes it a good fit behind server-sent events and websockets, where the browser drops the connection all the time and wants to continue where it was.

Since it is a table, you can filter on your own columns, here userId. Kafka cannot do that for you. Old messages are deleted on a timer after the retention time.

items.title: What it is not
items.text:
It is not Kafka. There are no partitions and no consumer groups, and the throughput is whatever one MySQL table gives you. If the volume grows by a factor of a hundred, this is the wrong tool and I will have to say so.

I still feel a bit like I am getting away with something.

Update, November 2026: it never had to be replaced. It has carried every use we have had for it, also for the largest customers.

items.title: A map tile as a 64-bit integer
items.text:
I want to know where users are, and I do not want to know where users are.

Both are true. Aggregates by area are useful: how many, where, when. An exact position per user is a liability. It is sensitive, and once it is stored it has to be protected for as long as it exists.

A quadkey solves most of this. It comes from the Bing Maps tile system. The world is one square, split in four, and each of those in four again. Every split adds one digit from 0 to 3, so a position at zoom level 18 is a string of 18 digits:

Each split adds one digit. The tile 213 is inside 21, which is inside 2. 0 1 3 20 22 23 Key As bits 2 10 21 10 01 213 10 01 11 Two bits per digit. A shorter key is a larger square, and a prefix of every key inside it. 

final Coordinate c = new Coordinate(40.757678, -73.969558);
QuadKey qk = new QuadKey(c, 18);     // about 0.6 m per pixel
qk.getAsString();                    // "032010110132031203"
qk.getAsLong();                      // 15104861027

Two things follow from how it is built.

A tile's key is a prefix of every tile inside it. So "is this point inside that square" is a prefix check, and on the integer form it is plain arithmetic. That makes it a good database index. A range scan on one indexed column finds everything in an area, with no spatial extension.

QuadKey qk = new QuadKey(c1, 16);
qk.contains(c2);                     // true

And the precision is something you choose. Cut the key at a lower zoom level and the position becomes a square of a few hundred meters, or a few kilometers. You store the square. The exact position is never written down, so it cannot leak later.

That is the part I like. It is not anonymisation, and I will not call it that. A square with one person in it is still that person. But it lets me decide the resolution up front, and keep what the aggregate needs and no more.

jquad is a small Java library for this. Each digit takes 2 bits, so a key fits in a 64-bit integer with room to spare.
path: A map tile as a 64-bit integer

items.title: A screen saver for a Chromecast, to save a plasma TV
items.text:
I have a plasma TV and a Chromecast, and they do not like each other.

When nothing is playing, the Chromecast goes to Backdrop mode. It shows nice photos, and on top of them a clock and some text that never move. A plasma is not very happy about non-moving images over time. The same goes for a paused programme that someone forgot.

There is no setting to turn it off. For a device that is made to sit on a TV all day, that is a strange thing to leave out. So I wrote a small Python script that watches the Chromecast. When it has been in Backdrop, or idle or paused, for too long, the script starts the default player with something random from a list of media URLs. When someone starts to watch something, it gets out of the way.

21:35:23 - Dicovered chromecast devices: ['LivingRoom']
21:35:58 - Discovered idle/paused player
21:36:03 - Discovered active player, resetting idle timer
21:40:43 - Discovered idle/paused player
21:41:43 - Current application has been idle too long, starting screensaver

It works with the default media player, NRK TV and TV 2 Sumo. It does not work with Netflix or HBO Nordic. Their media status cannot be read, so the script cannot tell a paused film from a playing one, and I would rather have burn-in than a screen saver in the middle of a film.

It is castsaver, built on PyChromecast, which did all the hard work. Not the cleanest code I have written. I spent an evening on a script to protect a TV from a 35 dollar gadget, and I am fine with that.

Update, November 2026: it ran for a couple of years.
path: A screen saver for a Chromecast, to save a plasma TV

items.title: A stopwatch you can leave on in production
items.text:
I like profilers. I also cannot use one where I need it most, which is in production, on the request that is slow right now.

A profiler tells you things you did not think to ask about, and that is what makes it good. It also slows the application down, and it changes what it measures. You do not attach one to a live system just because an export is slow.

What I can do in production is the dumb thing. Take the time before and after each step, add it up, and print it.

So Chronograph is a stopwatch with names.

final Chronograph chronograph = Chronograph.create();
chronograph.timed("lookup", this::lookup);
chronograph.timed("transform", this::transform);
System.out.println(chronograph.prettyPrint());

A task can be timed many times, and you get the average, the total, the count and the share of the whole:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| Task                  | Average      | Total        | Invocations   | %      |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| lookup                |    188.88 μs |     37.048 s |       196,143 |  79.7% |
| transform             |     32.62 μs |      6.398 s |       196,143 |  13.8% |
| sort                  |    306.97 ms |    306.97 ms |             1 |   0.7% |
| xml                   |     16.68 ms |     16.68 ms |             1 |   0.0% |
| serializing           |      1.677 s |      1.677 s |             1 |   3.6% |
| gzip-compressing      |      1.043 s |      1.043 s |             1 |   2.2% |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| Total: 46.489 s                                                              |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Look at lookup. 189 microseconds is nothing. Nobody would look twice at it. Done 196,143 times it is 37 of the 46 seconds. The slow-looking steps, the sort and the gzip, are noise next to it.

A profiler would have found that too. But this table can go in a log line, behind a switch, and be turned on when someone asks. That is the whole point of it for me.
path: A stopwatch you can leave on in production

items.title: What it cannot do
items.text:
It only measures what I thought to wrap. If the time goes somewhere I did not name, the table adds up to less than the request took and does not say why. A profiler has no such blind spot.

Added later: output from February 2025. Tasks can be nested now, and the time no named task covers is shown as <overhead>. Here that is 300 of the 516 ms in the request.

And System.nanoTime() has nanosecond resolution, not nanosecond precision. For steps that take microseconds or more that does not matter. For real micro-benchmarks, use JMH.
path: A stopwatch you can leave on in production

items.title: A study buddy that refuses to give the answer
items.text:
We built it in about an hour. Agreeing on what to build took most of the day.

This was at Claude Impact Lab in Oslo on 21 October. The idea was a study buddy for pupils, with one rule: it does not give the answer.

That sounds like a small rule. It is the opposite of what these models do by themselves. Ask one a maths question and you get the answer, worked out and explained, before you have thought at all. For homework that is close to useless. The pupil gets the answer and learns nothing.

So tenkemakker has a ladder of hints. The first is small, a nudge towards where to look. Ask again and you get a bit more. It moves up one step at a time, and it stops before the answer.

Then comes the part I like best. When the pupil has it, the roles are turned. The bot plays the one who does not understand, and the pupil has to teach it back. You do not know a thing until you can explain it, and a bot is a patient audience.
path: A study buddy that refuses to give the answer

items.title: What I learned
items.text:
Building it was the easy part. Once we were aligned on what it should do, it took an hour.

I am used to the opposite. In my work the idea is cheap and the building takes months, so we spend little time on the idea and a lot on the code. Here the cost has moved. When the building takes an hour, the time spent agreeing on a good idea is the work.

I found that uncomfortable, and I still do. The part I am good at is the part that just got cheap.
path: A study buddy that refuses to give the answer

items.title: Back to the world
items.text:
I thought that since it feels pretty late to enter the blogosphere at my age, I will write up a small explanation, if there is anyone interested.

As I have always had a passion for things that are fast (being code or vehicles), I started a site where I was writing tweak guides for games, especially FPS games. Back in ‘99, as I realized that many of these games (Quake, Half-Life, and a year later Unreal Tournament) had simple text based config files, I decided to write my first program to simplify the task.

The tool of choice was Visual Basic, and after the cstweak, q3tweak and uttweak programs were written, I started to write a simple browser for servers of multi-player games, this time in Java. Anyway, the effort of the project was kind of lost when GameSpy emerged.

Since then I have written a ton of hobby projects, including phone blog software (Phoggy), SMS ad tracking/target software, CMS systems in PHP and Python++. A lot of it has been lost (some of it for the better). I have not had a “blog” since 2004, so I thought it was about time to let the world know I’m alive.

items.title: Balanced ventilation in a house from 2000, with no visible ducts
items.text:
I spent a month putting balanced ventilation into our house, and I made the job about twice as big as it needed to be. On purpose.

The house is from 2000. It is tight enough that air does not leak in by itself, and it had no real ventilation. That is the worst of both. A tight house is what you want for the heating bill, and then you sit in the same air all winter.

We had three reasons to do something. The radon readings were on the border of the limit. There is asthma in the family. And the old system was one Villavent fan shared by the cooker hood, the bathrooms and the laundry room, so smell from one room ended up in the next.

So in June and July 2025 I put in a Flexit L6 SW with a rotating heat exchanger, rated at up to 95%. It stands in the attic. The ducts are spiro in 125, 160 and 200 mm with 50 mm of insulation, about 65 meters of it, run through the attic and down through one chase in a wall.

The unit in the attic, before the ducts were connected.
path: Balanced ventilation in a house from 2000, with no visible ducts

items.title: The over-ambition
items.text:
The normal design is simple. Fresh air goes into bedrooms and living rooms and is pulled out from bathrooms and the kitchen. Air moves between the rooms under the doors.

I did not want that. I wanted each room to be self-sufficient, so a room with the door shut still gets what it needs. Most rooms therefore have both a supply and an extract valve.

That doubles the ducting. In an existing house it also means ducts that have to cross each other in places that were never built for one duct, let alone two.

200 and 160 mm spiro duct.

And I had a second demand that pulled the other way. Nothing was to be visible. No lowered ceilings and no boxes along the walls. So I wanted twice the ducts and none of them in sight, in a house that was finished 25 years ago.

Two insulated ducts going down through an opened wall. The wall was closed again afterwards.

Would I do it again? Yes, I would. I will get to why when the valves are set, since that is where the extra ducts are supposed to pay off.
path: Balanced ventilation in a house from 2000, with no visible ducts

items.title: The joke
items.text:
I assume the work alone would be 200,000 NOK from a contractor, and likely more with this layout. I paid for parts.

Enova supports balanced ventilation in houses with a building permit from before July 2010. Ours qualifies. But the criteria require that professionals do the installation. So if you pay someone for the standard job, you get support. If you plan, build and measure a more thorough one yourself, you get nothing, however well it performs.

I got no support. That is a joke, tbh.
path: Balanced ventilation in a house from 2000, with no visible ducts

items.title: What is left
items.text: The system runs, but the valves are not set yet. Until they are, I have a lot of duct and no proof that it was worth it.
path: Balanced ventilation in a house from 2000, with no visible ducts

items.title: 44 watts for 200 m³/h: balancing the ventilation myself
items.text:
The extra ducts paid off. Balancing the ventilation was simple.

In June I gave almost every room both a supply and an extract valve, which doubled the ducting. The idea was that each room could be set by itself. In August I got to find out.

I borrowed a flow hood and a flow meter from a friend. It is professional equipment, the kind used for the protocol a contractor hands over. Then I measured every valve in the house.
path: 44 watts for 200 m³/h: balancing the ventilation myself

items.title: One room at a time
items.text:
With the normal design, air goes in in one room and out in another, so turning one valve changes the rest. Here a room with both valves gets out what it gets in. I could set one room, close the door and go to the next.

Room Supply (m³/h) Extract (m³/h) Living room 1 45.0 Living room 2 45.5 Loft living room 42.0 Gym 55.0 55.0 Bedroom 1 52.0 52.0 Bedroom 2 30.0 30.0 Bedroom 3 30.0 30.0 Laundry room closed 50.0 Bathroom 1 43.0 Bathroom 2 40.0 Sum 299.5 300.0

That is normal mode: 300 m³/h in and out, for a house of 141 m² and about 300 m³. So the air is replaced once an hour, for 78 watts.

For each valve I wrote down the number of turns from closed. If someone turns one by accident, it can be set back without measuring again.

Where the ducts meet in the attic, insulated.
path: 44 watts for 200 m³/h: balancing the ventilation myself

items.title: The modes
items.text:
Supply air per mode, m³/h, with the power it takes Required minimum 170 m³/h Away 195 m³/h, 44 W Normal 300 m³/h, 78 W High 358 m³/h, 111 W Higher 460 m³/h, 190 W

The lowest mode moves about 200 m³/h for 44 watts. The requirement for this house is about 170. So the setting for when nobody is home is above the minimum, for less than an old light bulb.

The highest mode is the opposite. 190 watts is 2.4 times the power of normal, for 1.5 times the air. It is for cooking and showers, not for running all day.

Extract is slightly higher than supply in every mode, from 0.5 to 14 m³/h. That is on purpose. A small underpressure keeps moist indoor air from being pushed into the walls. The two fans also need different speeds for the same flow, 47% and 50% in normal mode, which I would not have guessed.
path: 44 watts for 200 m³/h: balancing the ventilation myself

items.title: What I did not measure
items.text:
I measured every valve to half a cubic meter. The heat recovery I did not measure at all. 95% is the manufacturer's upper figure, and it is the number the whole unit is sold on.

So I was careful with the part I had borrowed tools for, and took the rest on trust. Winter will show.
path: 44 watts for 200 m³/h: balancing the ventilation myself

items.title: Watching it afterwards
items.text:
The house has three pressure sensors of my own now. Two sit on the 200 mm main ducts, in and out. A third, much more sensitive one is mounted in the attic floor and measures the difference between the large open room and the attic. They report to Home Assistant, so I can see live how the system is doing.

One of the sensors on its own page, in June while I was still building.

The duct sensors are Sensirion SDP810, a differential pressure sensor that speaks I²C. Four wires. Note that the datasheet draws the pins from below.

The four pins of the SDP810, seen from belowSDApin 4SDA I²C dataGNDpin 3GND groundVDDpin 2VDD supplySCLpin 1SCL I²C clock

Added later: the dashboard on 27 September 2025, in normal mode. Supply duct 20.5 Pa, extract duct -36.4 Pa, and -0.6 Pa between the house and the attic. The unit reported 84% heat recovery that day, with 15.8 °C outside.

Update, November 2026: it has run since without problems.

items.title: Five bugs in my own gateway in one day
items.text:
On 18 September I filed five bugs against my own gateway. I had not found any of them myself. An AI review did, in code I have run since 2023.

I had not expected much. The code is not new, it has been reviewed, and it has carried real traffic for years.

This is what I got.

A write to the file that captures request and response bodies could be short. AsynchronousFileChannel.write is allowed to write only part of the buffer, and my code completed after one callback. The rest was never written. So the tail of a captured body could be missing, with no error.

Upstream services that were removed from the configuration kept serving their routes. Forever, until restart.

An upstream that closed the connection in the middle of a response left buffer files behind, and the access log said 200 for a response the client never got in full.

A malformed Content-Type header threw an exception in the logging code, so the request that most deserved a log entry got none.

And the ClickHouse connection pool was never closed.
path: Five bugs in my own gateway in one day

items.title: What bothers me
items.text:
Look at the first one. This gateway exists to answer what a client sent us. And the capture could drop the end of the body without telling anyone. That is the one promise it makes.

I know that a write can be short. Everyone who has done I/O knows that. I still wrote the code as if it could not, and then read it many times without seeing it. It works in every test, since a short write to a local file almost never happens.

A person reviewing that code reads what it does. The machine seems to read what the API is allowed to do, and has the patience to check each call against it. I do not have that patience on the fifth file.
path: Five bugs in my own gateway in one day

items.title: What I take from it
items.text:
AI reviews are powerful. I say that with a smiley, and with some discomfort.

The second bug is worth a note of its own. It was a regression from another fix, and it was caught in the review of that fix. Before, the route map was wiped on every refresh, which cleaned up removed services as a side effect of a bug. I fixed the bug and lost the side effect.

All five are fixed.
path: Five bugs in my own gateway in one day

items.title: Generic API documenter for web-services
items.text:
For some time I have meant to fully document all the different APIs I’m involved in. It gives a more professional feel, it helps integrators and front-end developers and it actually makes it easier to spot inconsistencies in naming or configuration.

Most of our software is written in 100% Java 7 or 8. I was making an effort to find tools that could help me do this automatically, because nothing is worse than outdated and misleading documentation. And believe it or not, I do not like maintaining projects and code if I do not need to, so the hunt for a documentation tool started.

In short (mainly because I’m too lazy to write all my reasoning), I found the documentation tools to fall into on or more of the following three categories:

  • The produced documentation did not look very appealing
  • The lack of support for important parts of information (I want at least security roles, HTTP methods, URL, and optionally JavaDoc documentation or other information carved into the source code)
  • Too much hassle to setup or the tool trying to be an integral part of my software.
  • (Or last, not free/open source)

Now it sounds that I have (re-)invented the wheel and the best thing since sliced bread, and it may very well not be, however I believe this project fills a gap.

The strategy I have used is to create an independent model using an APT processor in the form of ethlo api-documenter. This outputs the model as a JSON file.

items.title: Geo lookups without a database
items.text:
In May I imported the world into MySQL. In October I deleted the database, and the library got simpler.

The data is the world. GeoNames has the places, with their names, coordinates and the hierarchy from continent down to town. GeoLite2 maps IP ranges to locations. I wanted one library that answers the simple questions: where is this IP, what is near this point, is this town inside that county.

I put it in a database, as I do with data. Import the files, add spatial indexes, write queries. It worked, and it had all the usual company. A schema, an import that took its time, encoding trouble on the build server, and a database that had to be running before a single test could.

Then I looked at what the data is. It changes when I download a new file, and at no other time. Nobody writes to it. There are no transactions and no concurrent updates, and nothing has to survive a crash, since the source files are still there.

Everything a database is good at, I was not using. I was using it as a slow way to read a file.

The commit log from October tells the rest:

2017-10-13 Load IP and locations into memory for maximum performance
2017-10-16 All geometry is removed from DB, and using inmem+file instead
2017-10-22 Rempved all SQL databases and use pure in.memory structures and files
2017-10-23 Now writing a dedicated MBR file on data import to make loading/startup a lot faster

geodata now reads its data from files into structures made for each question. IP ranges are sorted, so a lookup is a binary search. For "what is near this point", each boundary has a bounding rectangle, and those are checked before any real geometry is touched. The whole thing is a few hundred megabytes.

items.title: It turned into something else
items.text:
I should admit that this stopped being about geo data somewhere along the way. Once the database was gone, every lookup became a question of which structure fits, and I spent more time on that than the library needed.

For deployment it paid off. There is nothing to install and nothing to migrate.

A database is still the right answer when the data changes. This data does not.

items.title: Parsing ISO-8601 21 to 67 times faster than java.time
items.text:
In September 2026 I spent three days making a date parser faster. It already took less than a microsecond.

ITU is my library for the timestamps machines send each other, RFC 3339 and the ISO-8601 subset around it. It has existed since 2017.

After the three days, 1.16.0 parses a timestamp in 18 to 28 ns. java.time needs 542 to 577 ns for the same input on the same JDK. That is 21 to 30 times faster, and lenient parsing ends up 46 to 67 times faster. Nothing is allocated when you parse from a char[] or byte[].

Slowest input per operation, ns/op. Lower is better. parse, ITU 28 ns parse, JDK 577 ns parseLenient, ITU 17 ns parseLenient, JDK 788 ns formatSeconds, ITU 16 ns formatSeconds, JDK 100 ns formatNanos, ITU 33 ns formatNanos, JDK 115 ns parseDuration, ITU 52 ns parseDuration, JDK 247 ns

Measured with JMH on an i9-13900H laptop on JDK 25.0.4. The full report has every input with error bars.
path: Parsing ISO-8601 21 to 67 times faster than java.time

items.title: Does it matter?
items.text:
For one timestamp, no, it does not. Half a microsecond is nothing.

I tell people to measure before they optimise, and to stop when it is fast enough. By that rule I should have stopped years ago. I did not, since I like this kind of work, and I will not pretend the reason is better than that.

There is a real case too. A service that parses several timestamps per request, or a phone that parses thousands in one sync, pays that half microsecond every time. But that is the excuse and not the reason.
path: Parsing ISO-8601 21 to 67 times faster than java.time

items.title: Throwing away the numbers
items.text:
I have tuned this parser several times over the years. Each time I measured, kept what helped and threw away the numbers.

So I could not say what I had already tried. This time I kept a log of every attempt with its numbers, kept or not. It has a section called "Dead ends, do not retry without a new reason". Writing fields into the buffer as soon as they were parsed is in there. It looked obvious and gained nothing.

For someone who goes on about measuring, that took a long time to learn.
path: Parsing ISO-8601 21 to 67 times faster than java.time

items.title: How it got fast
items.text:
No single trick. The parser knows the format, so it reads digits at fixed positions instead of asking a formatter what comes next. An input of 19 characters or more takes a path with no per-field length checks. Dates are converted to day counts with Ben Joffe's algorithm. When formatting, digits are written two at a time from a table, straight into the caller's buffer.

Validation is the odd one. isValid on bad input is hundreds of times faster than the JDK, and it is not due to anything clever. The JDK builds an exception with a stack trace to tell you no. ITU returns false.
path: Parsing ISO-8601 21 to 67 times faster than java.time

items.title: Where it loses
items.text:
Formatting a duration is on par with the JDK, and slower for some inputs. It is in the report with the rest.

ITU also does less. No locales, no patterns, no calendars other than ISO. If you need those, this is not the library. And Instant.parse, the fastest built-in path, is in the benchmark too, so the comparison is not against the slowest thing I could find.

The benchmarks are in date-time-wars. Run them on your own hardware before you believe mine.
path: Parsing ISO-8601 21 to 67 times faster than java.time

items.title: JSON Schema to XSD
items.text:
Everyone is moving from XML to JSON. I just wrote a tool that goes the other way.

I am not nostalgic about XML. But a lot of systems still describe their services with an XML schema, also when the payloads themselves are JSON. So you end up with one definition in JSON Schema, and the need for the same thing as XSD on the other side. Writing both by hand means they will drift apart, and you find out when a message is rejected.

So I generate one from the other. jsons2xsd takes a JSON Schema and gives you an XSD.

final Config cfg = new Config.Builder()
    .targetNamespace("http://example.com/myschema.xsd")
    .name("array")
    .build();
final Document doc = Jsons2Xsd.convert(reader, cfg);

A property like this:

"name": {
  "type": "string",
  "minLength": 5,
  "maxLength": 32
}

becomes this:

<element name="name">
  <simpleType>
    <restriction base="string">
      <minLength value="5" />
      <maxLength value="32" />
    </restriction>
  </simpleType>
</element>

Required properties become plain elements, and optional ones get minOccurs="0". date-time becomes dateTime, and number becomes decimal.

That was the easy part. The two do not think alike. JSON Schema says what a value may be. XSD says what a document looks like, in order. A JSON number has no size, and XSD wants to know if it is an int or a long. Arrays are natural in one and a repeated element in the other. Not everything survives the trip, and I have only done the parts I need.

Update, November 2026: it became my most starred repository. The issues over the years were about what I guessed in 2013: arrays, simple types and int64.

#!/bin/sh
set -e

if [[ $# != 2 ]] ; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <source-repo> <destination-repo>"

fi

tmpdir=`mktemp -d 2>/dev/null || mktemp -d -t 'tmpdir'`

items.title: My own benchmark refused to publish my numbers
items.text:
I built a benchmark that decides by itself whether its numbers can be published. On the run I wanted to publish, it said no.

I do not trust gateway benchmarks much, mine included. It is too easy to get a nice number. Run the load generator on the same cores as the gateway, leave turbo on, pick the run that looked best, and you have a figure that nobody can reproduce, including you.

So the benchmark for r7 is one command, and it is strict with me.

It measures the published image, by digest, and not something I built on my laptop. wrk and wrk2 are built from pinned commits. The host is tuned first: SMT and turbo off, the performance governor, and every other process moved to housekeeping cores. nginx as backend, the gateway and the load generator each get cores of their own. wrk finds the saturation throughput, and wrk2 holds a fixed rate, so the p99 is free of coordinated omission.

There are two baselines. One has no gateway, which shows what the proxy hop costs in total. The other is r7 in the path with no filters and no journal. What a filter or a journal level costs is quoted against the second one, since it has the same topology and the same contention, and the noise cancels.

And every report opens with a verdict, PUBLISHABLE or NOT PUBLISHABLE. A dirty tree, a tuning step that did not apply, a missing run, or a backend that is not at least 10% faster than every r7 row, and the verdict is no.
path: My own benchmark refused to publish my numbers

items.title: The run of 11 October
items.text:
NOT PUBLISHABLE.

My first reaction was that the verdict was wrong. That is the reaction the verdict is there for, so I read the reasons.

There were three. nginx as a peer had reached the backend's own limit, so its number was the backend's and not nginx's. Spring Cloud Gateway could not hold the fixed 20,000 requests per second at all. And r7 itself could not hold that rate on the browser page with full journaling, where it saturates at 14,900.

None of these is a broken measurement. They are results. A gateway that cannot hold the rate is a finding about the gateway. One of the three was about r7 itself, and I did not enjoy that one.

API GET, saturation in requests per second on two cores. nginx 60,300, the backend's limit r7 43,600 cloud-gateway 18,600

The nginx bar is the backend's number. That was the first of the three reasons.

But the rule as I wrote it called them failures. So I had two choices. I could publish anyway and explain. Or I could change the rule, in the open, and show both.

I changed the rule. A peer at the backend's limit and a fixed-rate run above capacity are now marked in the report as results, and do not fail the run. The published page has the original report with its NOT PUBLISHABLE at the top, and next to it the current verdict over the same result files.
path: My own benchmark refused to publish my numbers

items.title: Is that cheating?
items.text:
It might look like it. I wrote a gate, it stopped me, and I moved the gate.

I do not think it is, since the numbers did not change and both verdicts are there to read. But I notice that I only found the flaw in the rule when it stood between me and a result I wanted. Would I have looked as hard if it had said PUBLISHABLE on a bad run? I hope so.

The numbers come from one run. Every throughput figure carries the spread of its three repeats, and a difference smaller than that spread is not a finding. The benchmark page has all of it.
path: My own benchmark refused to publish my numbers

items.title: One change listener for Hibernate and EclipseLink
items.text:
When core data changes, something else has to happen. A cache entry must go, a search index must be updated, and an audit log wants to know what the value was before. I had one mechanism for all three in my previous job, and missed it in the new one. So I built it again from scratch.

Spring has events, and since 4.2 it can send them at the end of a transaction. Spring Data JPA has auditing, but it tells you who changed something and when. It does not tell you what the data was. Calling that auditing is generous.

The persistence frameworks do know. Each of them has its own way of telling you, and none of them agree. Hibernate has interceptors. EclipseLink has descriptor listeners. Write your audit log against one, and you have married it.

Dachs, the Data Change Snitch, sits in between. It collects everything that is created, updated and deleted inside a transaction, and hands it over as one change set:

public interface EntityChangeSetListener
{
    void preDataChanged(EntityDataChangeSet changeset);
    void postDataChanged(EntityDataChangeSet changeset);
    void begin();
}

preDataChanged runs just before commit, and an exception there aborts the transaction. postDataChanged runs just after. That split matters. The audit log belongs before commit, since a change that cannot be logged should not happen. The cache and the search index belong after, since they must not hear about a change that was rolled back.
path: One change listener for Hibernate and EclipseLink

items.title: Why not use what is there?
items.text:
That is the fair question. Hibernate Envers does auditing. Each cache has its own invalidation.

But those are three mechanisms for one fact, that this entity changed from this to that. I would sooner have the fact once and let three listeners use it.

It supports Hibernate and EclipseLink so far.
path: One change listener for Hibernate and EclipseLink

items.title: One drop from model to print
items.text:
I wanted printing to be as simple as dropping a file on a page. To get there I had to make every decision the slicer normally asks about, once, on behalf of someone who does not want to be asked. That someone is me.

A slicer has hundreds of settings. I understand a fair share of them, and I do not want to see them when I print a cable clip. What I want to say is: this model, PETG, go.

So printdrop is a web page with a drop zone. Drop an STL or a 3MF. It slices headless with OrcaSlicer, picks the CFS slot that holds the right material, checks the printer and starts the print. That is the whole user interface for the normal case.

A dropped model. Filament, quality and Print.

curl -F file=@part.stl -F material=PETG -F slot=auto http://printer-host/api/jobs

The simple page hides a lot of opinions. Which profile, which layer height, whether the bed is warm enough to skip part of the start routine. I decided that the bed counts as warm if it is within 10 °C of the target, or the last print ended less than 20 minutes ago. Is that right? It is right for me, most of the time, and that is the trade. One decision made well enough is worth more to me than a setting.
path: One drop from model to print

items.title: The first print
items.text:
The first print went fine for 99% of the way and then stopped. It sat there, paused, with the nozzle held at 140 °C.

The cause was almost funny. At the end of a print, the printer cuts the filament and pulls it back into the CFS. The filament sensor saw the filament go away and did what it is there to do. It reported a runout and paused the print, at the last line of it.

So the end macro now turns the sensor off before the cut, and it is on during the print, where a real runout should still pause.

That one mistake says something about the whole idea. Everything I hide from the page I have to get right in the macros, since nobody is looking at a setting that would have shown the problem.
path: One drop from model to print

items.title: Where the time goes
items.text:
A short print on this printer is mostly not printing. It heats, homes, cleans the nozzle, loads filament and purges. So the start macro heats bed, nozzle and chamber at the same time and homes once. The end macro leaves the filament in the toolhead by default, and the next print with the same slot skips a load of about 70 seconds.

The macros print a marker at each phase, and the page shows a bar per job with the seconds for each. I did that before optimising anything, so I would know what was worth doing.

While it prints.
path: One drop from model to print

items.title: What it checks before the nozzle moves
items.text:
Klipper must be ready, the macros must be present and the printer must be idle. If the macros are gone, which a firmware update can do, it puts them back, but only when the printer is idle.

It is a tool for one printer and one person. Anything else it refuses, which is why it is simple.
path: One drop from model to print

items.title: Race standings from lap times alone
items.text:
RC racing has timing that tells you one thing: when each car crossed the line. I wanted to know who was ahead in the middle of a lap, and you cannot know that. It turns out you can get close enough.

In real motorsport you get GPS and sector times. In RC there is a loop at start/finish, and a list of lap times per driver afterwards. I film my races, and a video of one car going round is not very interesting to anyone but me. With the standing and the gap to the car ahead on screen, it is.

So the question was how much you can tell from lap times alone.

More than I thought. Add up a driver's laps and you know exactly when they crossed the line each time. Do that for everyone and you know the order and the gaps at every crossing. Between the crossings you do not know anything, so there I assume each car spends the lap at an even pace. That is wrong in every single lap, since nobody drives evenly, and somebody always crashes.

It was surprisingly good anyway. The errors are inside one lap and they are corrected at the next crossing, so they never build up.
path: Race standings from lap times alone

items.title: Subtitles as an overlay
items.text:
I did not want to write a video overlay. So LapStats writes an SRT file, the plain subtitle format, with the stats every time the driver passes start/finish. Any player can show it and YouTube takes it as it is. There is a JavaScript and HTML renderer as well, for when it should look better.

The data comes from MyRCM, the timing system used at the races.

One with rendering, and one with subtitles. I think it made the videos much more interesting to watch. That may say more about the videos.
path: Race standings from lap times alone

items.title: Rate limit IPv6 by the /64, not the address
items.text:
My gateway had a rate limiter that did nothing for IPv6 clients. I wrote it, and I should have known better.

The limiter in r7 is a token bucket per client, and the client was the IP address. For IPv4 that is fine. One address is roughly one client, or one office behind NAT.

For IPv6 it is wrong, and not by a little. A subscriber is normally given a whole /64. That is 2⁶⁴ addresses, about 18 quintillion, and the client can use any of them. So a client that wants to get past the limit takes a new address for every request, and gets a new, full bucket each time.

An IPv6 address. Documentation prefix, not a real one. 2001:0db8:1234:5678 xxxx:xxxx:xxxx:xxxx 64 bits from the provider 64 bits the client picks one subscriber, and now one bucket was one bucket per value

It is worse than no limit. The limiter keeps a bucket per address in memory, up to max_buckets. So the same client that walks past the limit also fills the table and pushes out the buckets of everyone else.

This is kinda humiliating. It is not obscure. I have known how IPv6 addresses are handed out for years, and I still wrote "per address" without thinking, the way I have always done it for IPv4.
path: Rate limit IPv6 by the /64, not the address

items.title: The fix
items.text:
IPv6 clients are now keyed by the leading 64 bits. IPv4 clients are keyed by the full address as before.

rate_limiter:
  capacity: 100
  refill_tokens: 100
  refill_period: 1s
  ipv6_prefix_length: 64

64 is the default, so you do not have to set it. You can lower it to 56 or 48 if you see providers that hand out more than a /64 per customer.

It was fixed before the first beta. If you have a rate limiter of your own, look at what it uses as the key.
path: Rate limit IPv6 by the /64, not the address

items.title: README examples that cannot rot
items.text:
I change my APIs a lot. I like to work on the API and the implementation at the same time, and move things until they feel right. The README is what pays for that.

An example in a README is code that no compiler sees. Rename a method and the tests fail, the build fails, and the README says nothing. It keeps showing the old name to everyone who visits, and those are the people who know the least about the library and trust the README the most.

I have shipped wrong examples that way. The honest fix is to be more careful, and I know myself well enough to not rely on that.

So the examples are now tests. They live in a package under src/test/java, they compile and they run. source-extractor-maven-plugin reads those files at build time, takes the body of each method, and puts it into the README through a template.

/**
 * The simplest and fastest way to parse an RFC-3339 timestamp by far!
 */
@Test
void parseRfc3339()
{
    final String text = "2012-12-27T19:07:22.123456789-03:00";
    final OffsetDateTime dateTime = ITU.parseDateTime(text);
    assertThat(dateTime.toString()).isEqualTo(text);
}

The method name becomes the heading, the Javadoc becomes the description, and the body becomes the code block, with a link to the line in the source. The README in the repository root is generated, and the one I edit is a template.

It took three days from the first commit to a release, and itu had its README rebuilt from it the same week.

items.title: What it does to the examples
items.text:
There is a cost. An example written as a test looks like a test. It has assertions in it, and it shows what the library returns by asserting it, where a hand-written example would have a comment. Some of mine read a bit stiff now.

It is also opinionated. It does one thing, in the way I wanted it, with Maven.

I will take stiff and correct.

items.title: Robot
items.text:
After a few days of writing code directly for drawing surfaces and cylinders, it turned out to be very hard work to get a good-looking robot. That gave me the idea of loading a model made in a 3D program instead. This gives much more flexibility when the models need updating, and it also makes it possible to set some material properties and light settings there, so that this does not have to be done by hand. The next step is to draw the robot's part models in the right position, and then animate the robot. The robot can be controlled either manually or through a control file, specified in XML.

I chose JOGL as the OpenGL implementation, since it is Java based, a language I feel I know well. That way I can spend my time on OpenGL code, and not have to learn a new programming language at the same time. The project started with a simple framework for the program. The framework consists of a window for OpenGL and a simple setup panel where you can see information about the graphics card and the machine, and also control the number of frames per second (fps) you want to show. The framework was easy to adapt, and from then on I only had to change the drawing routines to present graphics.

After a short while I realised that making a robot that looks like an industrial robot, hard-coded through OpenGL commands, would take a lot of time and be hard to update. Especially when updating individual parts of the robot. It would mean that e.g. swapping between different tools on the robot would be difficult if that kind of functionality was wanted later. So I started looking at how I could draw finished models loaded from file. OpenGL is only an API for drawing 2D and 3D, and has no support for anything like that, so I had to write the code for it myself.

items.title: Converting and loading models
items.text:
Once it was clear that I wanted to use drawn 3D models, I started looking for models of the robot. The robot at the IR department in Sarpsborg is from 92-93, so there was not much data to find about it on ABB's web pages. I went for a newer and more sophisticated robot instead. CAD models (production drawings) had already been made of this one. The drawings were available in a lot of formats, and many of the tools for working with them are unfortunately both extremely expensive and advanced. After testing about all the shareware versions of CAD software there are, I finally found the program "Rhinoceros", which could load a CAD model from the *.igs format. This program could also export the geometry as a 3D Studio MAX or LightWave file.

More conversion was still needed. 3D Studio MAX and Lightwave have relatively complex file formats, and I did not want to parse those directly. The next task was to find a suitable file format to read into the program, since most of these formats (3D Studio Max and Lightwave) are hard to read, and are often proprietary or without available documentation. A standard ASCII file format would be ideal for reading and parsing in Java, and after searching for a while I found the program MilkShape. It supports importing many well-known file formats and can export to a relatively simple ASCII format, which was also well documented. Milkshape is a simple modelling program originally made for working with models from the game Half-Life. Over time it has got support for many more formats, and a lot of people prefer it today because of the low price and because it is easy to use. Like most other 3D programs, Milkshape lets you set material properties and light properties, and it also supports textures. That way you can finish the model in the 3D program, and then use the geometry, material properties and texture names from the ASCII file to draw the model in OpenGL later. It should be mentioned that the models used are from construction drawings, and are therefore very detailed and relatively heavy to render in OpenGL without a proper graphics card.

Milkshape after loading a model of one of the parts of the robot.

After understanding the format, I had to find a decent way to represent the models internally as objects in the program. A scene consists of one or more models, which have one or more meshes, which can have a material, which can consist of surface values for reflection, colour etc. and possibly a texture. It turns out to be a small hierarchy of objects. To be able to build a scene in as clear a way as possible, I made classes that represent these.

Overview of how a scene is built up in the program.

I also made a separate Texture class. I chose PNG as the format for textures. The Texture class can be extended to support e.g. BMP and JPG, but I have not taken the time to do that. Since it is quite possible that several models use the same textures, I implemented a texture list so that access to a texture can be shared. This avoids loading a texture several times, which again gives faster startup and saves memory.

Note: The textures are under 'program/build/data/textures'. The models are under 'program/build/data/models'.

items.title: Drawing the robot
items.text:
When the geometry for the parts of the robot has been read in, the next step is to draw the model on the screen. Since these are fairly complex models, there are a lot of triangles to draw. Drawing everything through code every time, or putting it in a "display list", is supposedly not meant to make any difference to performance on modern graphics cards. Still, I saw a 30-40% performance increase in JOGL by using display lists. This may be because the display lists are buffered and drawn through native code in JOGL, so you avoid Java's memory handling and iteration when drawing.

When the program starts, it loads all the models and makes a list of which textures have to be loaded. When all the models are loaded, the next step is to load all the textures needed and give the references to them to each Mesh object that uses the given texture. The next step is to make the display lists for each model, as mentioned in the paragraph above. The Scene object keeps track of which ID the model has in the display list inside OpenGL, and you can get it out when you want to draw a model in OpenGL.

In code it looks like this:

// Load models
String modelPath = "data/models/";
String[] modelFiles = new String[]
{
    "foot.txt",
    "rotation.txt",
    "lower_arm.txt"
    "elbow.txt",
    "upper_arm.txt",
    "floor.txt",
    "mount.txt"
};
// Init scene
this.scene = new Scene();
for (int i = 0; i < modelFiles.length; i++)
{
    this.scene.addModel(new MilkShapeModel(modelPath + modelFiles[i], modelFiles[i]));
}

Now that all the models are loaded (textures too), we can prepare the scene for rendering. This is done by calling "prepareScene" in the Scene class from init in OpenGL:

public void init (GLDrawable drawable)
{
    // Save references
    this.gl = drawable.getGL();
    this.glu = drawable.getGLU();
    this.glDrawable = drawable;
    // Prepare scene
    this.scene.prepareScene(gl, glu);

This generates the display lists, and the OpenGL ids of the lists are stored in the Scene object so that we can find the right list for a model when we are going to draw it. The robot is drawn like this:

public void display(GLDrawable drawable)
{
    // Clear scene
    gl.glClear(GL.GL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT | GL.GL_DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT);
    // Reset view
    gl.glLoadIdentity();
    // Update view if user has rotated or zoomed the scene
      gl.glTranslatef(0.0f, -12.0f, zoom);
      gl.glRotated(xrot, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0);
    gl.glRotated(yrot, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0);
    // Draw models
    // Draw robot mount
    gl.glPushMatrix();
      gl.glTranslatef(-7.2f, 0f, -4.6f);
      gl.glScalef(0.3f, 0.3f, 0.4f);
    drawModel(scene.getDisplayListIndex("mount.txt"), gl);
    // Foot
    gl.glPopMatrix();
    gl.glPushMatrix();
    drawModel(scene.getDisplayListIndex("foot.txt"), gl);
    // Rotation model
    gl.glTranslatef(0.0f, 2.0f, 0.0f);
    gl.glRotatef(robotStatus.getAxisAngle(0), 0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f);
    drawModel(scene.getDisplayListIndex("rotation.txt"), gl);
    // Lower arm
    gl.glTranslatef(3.3f, 5.8f, 1.35f);
    gl.glRotatef(robotStatus.getAxisAngle(1), 0.0f, 0.0f, 1.0f);
    drawModel(scene.getDisplayListIndex("lower_arm.txt"), gl);
    ...

items.title: Controlling the robot
items.text:
The robot can be controlled in two ways. Either fully manually through the GUI, or it can be programmed in advance to perform a series of movements. Manual control of the robot should be fairly intuitive, so I will concentrate on automatic running. This is done by the robot reading an XML file with specifications of which movements to perform at which times. All joints can be moved independently of each other at the same time, at different speeds if that is wanted.

The file has a very simple format, and is best explained with an example:

<robotprogram axisCount="4">
    <move time="2000">
        <axis id="0" abs="0">-40.0</axis>
        <axis id="1" abs="0">-80.0</axis>
        <axis id="2" abs="0">80.0</axis>
        <axis id="3" abs="0">180.0,-180.0</axis>
    </move>
    <move time="2000">
        <axis id="0" abs="0">40.0</axis>
        <axis id="1" abs="0">80.0</axis>
        <axis id="2" abs="0">-80.0</axis>
        <axis id="3" abs="0">-180.0,180.0</axis>
    </move>
</robotprogram>

The file starts by specifying how many axes the robot has (axisCount="4"). Then comes the robot's first combined movement: Axis 0 is to rotate -40 degrees, axis 1 is to rotate -80 degrees and so on. All of this is to be done in the time given by the attribute "time" in the "move" element, in this case 2000 milliseconds. The attribute "abs" says whether the positions for the axes are relative or absolute. So far only relative positions are implemented.

When the robot is going to run such a "program", it first loads the whole file into memory and splits the movement into small fragments that are put in a multidimensional array. When the program has been processed, it can easily be run with a single program thread, since all the axis movements are already calculated. Unfortunately there is no editor for making the file automatically through e.g. a macro recorder. I hope to get this implemented in a future version.

items.title: Conclusion and further work
items.text:
The requirement for the project that was set at the start of the course should be met with this. Still, there is room for improvements and extensions. Seeing a robot do "real" tasks is of course tempting, but I have not given the robot any specific task, since e.g. moving objects would have to be hard-coded together with the movement of the robot. This could only have been solved by implementing physical laws, so that objects like crates, boxes etc. fall to the floor, and so that you can push things away if they are not too heavy and/or have too much friction. That is a big task in itself, and I have not had time for more than barely making a "shell" for how such functionality can be implemented. The project has become relatively solid, and should be a decent solution to build on. There is a fair bit of code (about 3000 lines), but the code is well commented and it should be possible to find your way around it. Many of the classes can be used for other things than robot animations. The classes are divided into "packages" by what they do, much like Java's own class library.

Further, as already mentioned, it would be nice to make a macro recorder that could record/edit all manual movements done with the robot, so that they can be saved and played back later as a normal XML "program". Since the code for loading new models is now this simple, it should be possible to build a reasonably believable environment where one or more robots work.

items.title: Rules that make an AI agent useful on side projects
items.text:
I have more side projects moving now than I ever had, since an AI agent does most of the typing. For a while I also had more things that did not work than I ever had.

The agent is fast and it is confident. It tells you a thing is built, and it is, in the sense that the code exists. Whether it runs is another matter.

So the projects have rules now. They are not clever. Most of them are what I would tell a new developer in the first week.

Never claim something is built unless it was run. This is the first one and the one that changed the most. "Done" has to come with what was run and what came out. A test that only prints a number is not a test.

Decisions are written down, with the reason. One file per decision, dated. The game project has 84 of them. The agent starts every session without memory, so without these it will propose the idea I rejected last week, with the same good arguments.

Findings go in a dated file. What was tried, what came out, kept or not. This includes the dead ends, and those are the most valuable. The same project has 202 experiment notes.

A design note is history. It says how we got here. It is read for the why and never as a description of the code as it is now.

One command builds it and one command tests it, and both are in the file the agent reads first.
path: Rules that make an AI agent useful on side projects

items.title: None of this is about AI
items.text:
Decision records, a lab notebook and "it is not done until it runs" are things I have known for a long time. I have also skipped them on my own projects for just as long, since I was the only one there and I remembered.

The agent does not remember, so I had to write it down. And now my side projects are better documented than a good part of what I have been paid to build.

That is a bit embarrassing.

items.title: Scripts inside a running JVM
items.text:
Every client wants one small thing that no other client wants. It is always a few lines of code, and it never belongs in the main code base.

You know the kind. One client needs three API calls done as one, in one transaction. Another needs a report that is too heavy and too odd to be a feature. Say yes to all of it and the core fills up with special cases. Say no and you are the reason the integration is late.

Lamebda is my way of saying yes somewhere else. It is a plugin system for a Spring application. You put a project folder next to the running application, with source files in it, Groovy or Java:

@RestController
class MyController {
    @GetMapping("/my/{id}")
    def get(@PathVariable("id") int id) {
        return [requested: id]
    }
}

The application compiles it, loads it and serves it under its own path. The script runs inside the JVM, so it can call the same services the core uses, in the same transaction. That is what you cannot get from an integration that lives outside and talks HTTP: several calls that either all happen or do not.

It is used for batching, for transactions across calls, and for the ad-hoc services behind complex and costly reports. The custom code can change every week and the core does not have to be released for it.

items.title: How isolated is it?
items.text:
Less than it looks. The code is out of the main repository, and that feels clean. But it runs in the same process, with the same database and the same memory. A bad script can take the application down as well as any code in the core can, and it has been through less review.

So the isolation is in the source and in the release cycle. At runtime there is none, and I should not pretend there is.

Each project gets one class loader of its own, so a project can be reloaded as a unit when its files change.

Update, November 2026: it is a slippery slope. When a component from a script gets registered with other parts of the application, the old class loader cannot be unloaded, and you get NoClassDefFoundError after a reload.

items.title: Seven releases in two weeks
items.text:
The library worked. I spent two weeks rewriting large parts of it anyway, and broke compatibility on the way.

itu parses and formats RFC 3339 timestamps. I wrote it in 2017, and it had been quiet for a long time. It has served us well, and that is a good state for a library to be in.

What changed is where it runs. It is used on Android phones now. On a server, a slow parser costs a bit of CPU that nobody sees. On a phone the same work is felt by every user. So there was more to gain, and it would have real impact.

Releases of itu, 2017 to March 2022. 201720182019202020212022 1.4.0 to 1.7.0, seven releases in 13 days a long gap

Between 26 February and 10 March there were seven releases, 1.4.0 to 1.7.0.

Formatting got a massive improvement in 1.5.0, and nearly doubled again in 1.5.2. The benchmarks were rewritten in JMH, since my old loop with a timer was not something I could defend any longer. Leap seconds are now checked against the list of known ones. And lenient parsing returns a DateTime of its own, so 2017-12-06 and 2017-12-06T12:30Z can both be parsed without pretending the first one has a time.

The plot from the 1.7.0 README.

items.title: The part I am less proud of
items.text:
1.5.0 has a breaking change in a minor version. Parsing null or an empty string used to return null. Now it throws, in line with the java.time classes. And 1.6.0 removed the methods for java.util.Date.

Both are right. A parser that answers null for nothing hides bugs, and java.util.Date should have been gone long ago. But a library that has been quiet for years is one that people have stopped watching. Then it wakes up, and a dependency bump breaks their build.

Should that have been a 2.0? Probably. I wanted the numbers out, and I did not want to wait for a major version to fix what I thought was a mistake from the start.

I would be annoyed at a library that did this to me.

items.title: Project: SleePy
items.text: A news system in Python, built on XML files instead of a database. Project in the course Programming for the web, spring 2003.

items.title: Concept (29.01.2003)
items.text:
I want to make a system that makes it possible to post news, articles and so on. In other words what is needed to run a news site for any topic. Since there are systems for this already, like newspro which I have used myself, I will try to make a system for importing these into my own system, and store them as xml.

Further, a system for authentication will be needed, so that only admins/superusers can post/edit news, articles or similar. Since I don't know exactly how much time this will take, it is hard to say what may get added or maybe removed in favour of something else.

The idea is that the user of the system does not need to know how to code, write html or have any technical knowledge about the Internet.

The system will be built on flat files, which means XML. I could have built it on a database too, but where is the challenge in that!? =] By using flat files you can get away with cheaper web hosting, and in smaller systems like this one, performance will not suffer enough to become a problem.

Other than that there is not much to say. It may not be the most original project, but it is something I need for my own use, so it could be interesting to see how far I manage to get...

items.title: The news format
items.text:
To try to stay on good terms with the standards, the standard set by the dublincore project is followed as far as possible. They define only 15 tags that are supposed to cover what is needed to handle/maintain metadata. Since XML is aiming to be/already is the standard for exchanging information between different systems, the point is to follow the standards that have been set.

For all the details see: http://dublincore.org/

items.title: Functionality
items.text:
This is functionality that is coming/already implemented:

NNTP news support:

  • Fetch news from an NNTP server
  • The group to fetch from can be chosen freely, but has to follow the same standard as NTB's newsgroups.
  • Present headlines/headlines with lead/the whole news item.

General functions for news:

  • Search by keyword
  • Get news by date
  • Post news
  • Edit news
  • Delete news
  • Post comments on news
  • News is stored in categories per day.

Framework/settings:

  • Almost all of the site will be template based. These templates will be built on XSLT/XHTML.
  • Python will be used to do the transformations.
  • Settings are stored as a separate xml document and can be edited by hand if wanted. Hopefully there will be time to finish the planned web interface for settings.

Users:

  • There are 3 types of users:
    • guest - Can only post comments. Can become members themselves.
    • user - the above, plus being able to post news and edit their own posted news. Created by admin.
    • admin - the above, plus making changes to settings. Created by admin.
  • Users are authenticated with cookies if they have logged in before.

Storing data:

  • News data is stored in the same format as the news posted on the site, namely XML. The news is stored in its own file, one per day, e.g. '030325_ntb.utenriks.nytt.xml', or '030325_development.xml'.
  • Settings are, as mentioned above, stored in an XML file.

Presentation:

  • The pages are built as XHTML pages following the strictest standard, XHTML 1.1 Strict.
  • Styles are maintained with CSS(2) and the structure of the pages with the template solution mentioned above.

Other:

  • This project will try to do what can be done to keep the performance of the system up. A bit of 'intelligence' will probably be added to the system for fetching data from the NNTP server and so on, to reduce the load on the server..
  • No database will be used, to keep the cost of web hosting low.
