items.title: Spring DefaultKeyGenerator gotcha
items.text:
To speed things up I had applied the excellent @Cacheable annotation to a service method in our application (don’t miss the excellent performance analysis here, btw). However, I had not paid too much attention to the parameters going into the cache key. I would have expected something like concatenated toString() or something similar, however the default is to use the hashCode() of each parameter and create another (32-bit) hash code. Obviously this can easily generate collisions, as we shall soon see.

The service method in my service class took two parameters, a long and an int:

@Cacheable
getData(long a, int b)

The test failed intermittently with an assertion error that the data returned was wrong, which baffled me, until I had a look at the DefaultKeyGenerator source code:

public Object generate(Object target, Method method, Object... params) {
    if (params.length == 1) {
        return (params[0] == null ? NULL_PARAM_KEY : params[0]);
    }
    if (params.length == 0) {
        return NO_PARAM_KEY;
    }
    int hashCode = 17;
    for (Object object : params) {
        hashCode = 31 * hashCode + (object == null ? NULL_PARAM_KEY : object.hashCode());
    }
    return Integer.valueOf(hashCode);
}

Truly simple input can be used to expose the problem:

System.out.println(new DefaultKeyGenerator().generate(null, null, 1, 0)); // 16368
System.out.println(new DefaultKeyGenerator().generate(null, null, 0, 31)); // 16368

Looking at the documentation of DefaultKeyGenerator, there is a mention of using the arguments’s hash codes, however I feel the risks should be better communicated. To not just sound like a grumpy old fart, I notified the Spring team.

items.title: Spring's transaction-aware cache has a massive flaw
items.text:
Spring has a decorator that keeps your cache honest when a transaction rolls back. It does that by lying to you until the transaction is over.

The idea is sound. If you write to a cache inside a transaction and the transaction rolls back, the cache holds a value that never existed in the database. So TransactionAwareCacheDecorator holds the write back until commit.

The problem is that it holds it back from you as well.

cache.put("foo", "bar");
cache.get("foo");   // null, until the transaction has committed

That one you notice. The other case is worse. The key already had a value, you update it, and every read for the rest of the transaction gives you the old one. There is no error and nothing in the log. Writing data and then reading it back gives you what was there before you wrote. I cannot think of a case where anyone wants that.

One transaction, with the key already cached as “old”. put(k, new) get(k) commit get(k) Spring Mine old new new new

So you turn on the safe option, and your code starts acting on stale data. Or it misses the cache every time and goes to the database, and the cache you added for speed does nothing in the place where you do most of the work.

The name says transaction aware, and I took that to mean what I wanted it to mean.
path: Spring's transaction-aware cache has a massive flaw

items.title: What I did instead
items.text:
spring-tx-cache-decorator keeps a transient cache for the length of the transaction. Reads look there first, then in the real cache. On commit the transient values are merged into the real cache. On rollback they are thrown away. The same goes for evict and clear: you see your own changes, and nobody else does until commit.

final Cache myCache = myCacheManager.getCache("my-cache");
final Cache wrapped = new EnhancedTransactionAwareCacheDecorator(myCache, cacheCacheResult);

This is the rollback test:

@Test
public void testInvokePutInsideTransactionWithRollback()
{
    mockTxnManager(true);
    decoratorA.put("foo", "bar");

    // Make sure the transient cache holds this
    assertThat(decoratorA.get("foo", String.class)).isEqualTo("bar");

    // Should not yet be in the cache itself
    assertThat(realCacheA).doesNotContainKeys("foo");

    // Rollback
    mockTransactionEnd(false);

    // Make sure the cache does not hold it
    assertThat(decoratorA.get("foo", String.class)).isNull();
}

Knowing where the transaction starts and ends gave me one more thing. A value read from a remote cache can be kept in the transient one, so the second read in the same transaction costs a map lookup and no round trip. That is the cacheCacheResult flag. It is off by default, since it only helps when the same key is read more than once.
path: Spring's transaction-aware cache has a massive flaw

items.title: It is not a transactional cache
items.text: I should be careful here, since I just complained about a name that promises too much. This does not make your cache transactional. It only stops the real cache from being filled before commit. Isolation is roughly read committed: when another transaction commits a change, you see it at once. There is no locking, and two transactions that write the same key both win, in commit order.
path: Spring's transaction-aware cache has a massive flaw

items.title: Why not fix it in Spring?
items.text:
It has been reported, as issue 17353. I assume the behaviour is kept for compatibility. A decorator of my own was quicker than waiting.

It still surprises me that this is the default.
path: Spring's transaction-aware cache has a massive flaw

items.title: The home network as a YAML file
items.text:
I have replaced the router and the core switch at home, and neither was set up by hand. The whole network is now one YAML file and an Ansible playbook.

The old setup was a consumer mesh router doing everything, and a switch that could only be set up by clicking in a web page. It worked. I also had no idea what I had clicked in it over the years, and which of those clicks the house depended on.

That is what bothered me. I had already put the home server in a repository, so it can be rebuilt from nothing. The network under it was the one part that only existed as settings inside a box.

So there is a new router and a new core switch, both MikroTik, and neither is set up by hand. One file describes the network: the devices, their fixed leases and names, and the rules. An Ansible playbook applies it to both boxes over their API.

ansible-playbook network.yml --check --diff     # dry run
ansible-playbook network.yml --diff

ISP boxRouterCore switch Home server, 10GWi-Fi access pointThe rest Cameras, PoE trunk

The two blue boxes are set up from the file.
path: The home network as a YAML file

items.title: The switch-over
items.text:
This was the part I was nervous about. You cannot test a router change from behind the router you are changing.

So the new router first ran in a staging mode, on its factory network, next to the old one. I could plug a laptop into it and check that it gave out addresses, answered DNS and reached the internet, while the house still ran on the old router. The switch-over was then one variable changed from staging to final, a playbook run, and some cables moved in the right order. The plan allowed for 15 to 30 minutes without internet.

What broke? Nothing really. The game server did not answer from inside the house afterwards, and that was all.

Two things I would tell someone doing the same. Give the old router a fixed address of its own when it becomes an access point, so it can never take the new router's address. And keep a way in that does not depend on the config being right. Each box still answers on its factory address from a cable until I remove that on purpose.
path: The home network as a YAML file

items.title: Is it over-engineering?
items.text:
For a network with one router, probably yes. I would say so if someone showed it to me at work. Nobody needs a dry run to add a DHCP lease.

But I can read the whole network in one file now, and see in a diff what changed and when. The next time something stops working, there is a file and a history to look at, where before there was only my memory.
path: The home network as a YAML file

items.title: The school's weekly plan in Home Assistant, without AI

items.title: Why not a language model?
items.text:
Reading a table out of a PDF and making calendar events is the kind of task you would hand to a language model today. I did not, for three reasons.

It is about children. The plans and messages have names in them, and I do not want to send that to a service to save myself some parsing.

It has to be the same every time. A parser that reads a plan gives the same events tomorrow as today. And when it cannot read a plan, it gives nothing. A model would give me something that looks right. A wrong gym day is worse than a missing one.

And the plans are not that varied. A plan is a table with the weekdays as columns. What is the same every day is left out, and what differs becomes an event. Rows that say when school ends give the end of the day, and the homework columns give homework.

So it is a script. Each file is read once.
path: The school's weekly plan in Home Assistant, without AI

items.title: What that costs
items.text:
The honest downside is that it only reads the layouts it has seen. A teacher who makes the plan in a new way gets a plan that comes out wrong, or not at all. A model would likely cope with that, and my parser needs a new test fixture.

PDFs are also not tables. They are text placed at positions, and the table is something your eye makes. The parser reads the text in layout mode and finds the columns again from the spacing, which is as fragile as it sounds.

I still think it is the right trade here. It is boring and predictable, and the data stays at home.

Logging in was the hard part, to be honest. BankID needs a real browser, and Home Assistant cannot log in by itself. So there is a Chromium container next to it, and you log in there from your phone. It is on GitHub if you are a parent in the same portal.
path: The school's weekly plan in Home Assistant, without AI

  • q3tweak for Quake 3 Arena

items.title: Using PHP and existing htpasswd-file for authentication
items.text: Our clients were a bit unhappy with the inability to log out from basic auth protected services. As I did not want to have everyone update their passwords (and having them kept in a file is actually flexible enough for such a small service), I wrote a small helper class to match username/password in the existing .htpasswd file.
path: Using PHP and existing htpasswd-file for authentication

items.title: HtpasswdAuth.php
items.text:
<?
class HtpasswdAuth
{
    private $passwdFile = NULL;

    function __construct($passwdFile)
    {
        $this->passwdFile = $passwdFile;
    }

    public function matches($username, $password)
    {
        $lines = file($this->passwdFile);
        foreach ($lines as $line)
        {
            $arr = explode(":", $line);
            $fileUsername = $arr[0];
            if ($fileUsername == $username)
            {
                $filePasswd = trim($arr[1]);
                if (strpos($filePasswd, '$apr1') === 0)
                {
                    // MD5
                    $passParts = explode('$', $filePasswd);
                    $salt = $passParts[2];
                    $hashed = $this->cryptApr1Md5($password, $salt);
                    return $hashed == $filePasswd;
                }
                else
                {
                    // Crypt
                    $salt = substr($filePasswd, 0, 2);
                    $hashed = crypt($password, $salt);
                    return $hashed == $filePasswd;
                }
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    // Slight adaption of http://www.php.net/manual/en/function.crypt.php#73619
    private function cryptApr1Md5($plainpasswd, $salt)
    {
        $len = strlen($plainpasswd);
        $text = $plainpasswd.'$apr1$'.$salt;
        $bin = pack("H32", md5($plainpasswd.$salt.$plainpasswd));
        for($i = $len; $i > 0; $i -= 16) { $text .= substr($bin, 0, min(16, $i)); }
        for($i = $len; $i > 0; $i >>= 1) { $text .= ($i & 1) ? chr(0) : $plainpasswd{0}; }
        $bin = pack("H32", md5($text));
        for($i = 0; $i < 1000; $i++) {
            $new = ($i & 1) ? $plainpasswd : $bin;
            if ($i % 3) $new .= $salt;
            if ($i % 7) $new .= $plainpasswd;
            $new .= ($i & 1) ? $bin : $plainpasswd;
            $bin = pack("H32", md5($new));
        }
        $tmp = '';
        for ($i = 0; $i < 5; $i++) {
            $k = $i + 6;
            $j = $i + 12;
            if ($j == 16) $j = 5;
            $tmp = $bin[$i].$bin[$k].$bin[$j].$tmp;
        }
        $tmp = chr(0).chr(0).$bin[11].$tmp;
        $tmp = strtr(strrev(substr(base64_encode($tmp), 2)),
        "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/",
        "./0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz");
        return "$"."apr1"."$".$salt."$".$tmp;
    }
}
path: Using PHP and existing htpasswd-file for authentication

items.title: Rudimentary usage example
items.text:
<?php

$auth = new HtpasswdAuth('/path/to/.htpasswd');

session_start();

if (strtolower($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']) == 'post')
{
    $username = isset($_POST['username']) ? $_POST['username'] : null;
    $password = isset($_POST['password']) ? $_POST['password'] : null;
    if ($auth->matches($username, $password))
    {
        $_SESSION['user'] = $username;
    }
    else
    {
        die ('Incorrect username or password');
    }
}
else if (isset($_REQUEST['logout']))
{

}

</html>

items.title: Waiting for transaction propagation
items.text:
In the land of traditional ACID DBs, I often encounter code that is trying to collaborate with some external system using a queue or notification system. The problem is that it ends up sending the notification to the external system before the data has been committed to the central database. Then when the external system tries to query for data based on the notification, the data is not there yet (a different or outside a transaction).

The remedy I see most often is using a delay using Thread.sleep().

Why is this a problem? First of all you have no idea how long you may need to sleep, as it is affected by the transaction and data size and the amount of load on the database, so you will have to wait a long time just to be almost sure. The other problem you have now introduced is that all processes are now delayed for at least the amount of time the process waits.

This is probably known to many people already (but obviously not everyone), so here goes:

private SomeNotificationService delegate;

public void process(final Object event)
{
  TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(
    new TransactionSynchronizationAdapter()
    {
      @Override
      public void afterCommit()
      {
        delegate.sendEvent(event);
      }
    });
}

That’s it! Spring’s transaction handling will wait until the transaction is finished until it sends the notification (or not at all if the commit fails).

Simple, yet very powerful!

items.title: Weaving EclipseLink entities at build time
items.text:
EclipseLink needs to change your entity classes to do lazy loading and change tracking properly. It can do that when the application starts. That sounds convenient. It has been a pain in the neck on every server I have set it up on.

Load-time weaving needs a Java agent on the JVM command line, or an application server whose class loader does it for you. So how your entities behave depends on how the server was started. Forget the agent on one machine and everything still works, only slower, and with lazy relations that are not lazy. Nothing fails, so nobody notices.

That is the worst kind of failure. The code I tested should be the code that runs, and a startup flag should not decide it.

Static weaving does the same change at build time. The classes in the jar are already woven, and the server needs nothing. EclipseLink ships a tool for it, but wiring it into a Maven build is more XML than it should be, and you have to keep a persistence.xml with every entity class listed by hand. The compiler already knows which classes are entities.

So I wrote a plugin for it:

<plugin>
    <groupId>com.ethlo.persistence.tools</groupId>
    <artifactId>eclipselink-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <phase>process-classes</phase>
            <goals>
                <goal>weave</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

It finds the entity classes itself, so the persistence.xml does not need the list. A second goal, modelgen, generates the canonical metamodel without setting up an annotation processor.

It is a small thing. It should have been in EclipseLink. It is on GitHub.

Update, November 2026: I am still maintaining it, 13 years later. Most of the work has come from the outside moving, such as Spring Boot 3.1 and the Persistence 3.2 schema. It has never been a problem for me. The early adopters are the ones who get hit.

items.title: What an agent needs to know, I needed too
items.text:
I built a page to give an AI agent the context it needs for my work. The page turned out to be useful with no agent at all.

An agent that is going to help with a pull request needs to know things. Which PR, what the ticket says, who is waiting for whom, what the reviewer asked for last. A person on the team has that in their head, or thinks so. An agent has nothing, so you have to collect it and lay it out.

Clearsky is what came out of that. It is one local page with reviews, my PRs, tickets, mentions, today's meetings and a stand-up summary, and a coding agent in a sandbox next to it. It runs on 127.0.0.1 with the logins the machine already has. There are no tokens to make and no server.

The work list. The data is made up, as in all the screenshots here.
path: What an agent needs to know, I needed too

items.title: Whose move is it?
items.text:
To hand work to an agent I had to answer a question I had never answered for myself. What does "needs me" mean?

A review request does. A PR of mine with new comments does. A PR of mine that waits for someone else does not, and it should not sit in the same list. A bot is not a reviewer. A thread where I answered last is not mine any more.

Those are small rules. Written down, they turn five browser tabs into one list, sorted by whose move it is. Each row says the next step: review it, read the new commits, fix the failing checks, reply.

The stand-up is the same idea. An agent that should summarise my day needs to know what I did: PRs opened and reviewed, tickets moved, commits. Once that is collected, the summary is mostly there before any model has seen it.

Yesterday, from what actually happened.

I think that is the general point. Preparing information for an AI process means making it explicit, complete and in one place. That is good for the AI. It is also what a new colleague needs, and what I need on a Monday. We just never do it for people, since people cope.
path: What an agent needs to know, I needed too

items.title: The agent
items.text:
The chat runs GitHub Copilot CLI or Claude Code, in my clone of the repo, with the PR or ticket attached.

A chat on a PR.

I did not want to judge shell commands one by one. So Clearsky does not try. The agent runs in a sandbox that keeps it to my folders and a list of hosts, and a few doors lead out. Reading goes through. A push, a ticket change or a new host waits until I click Allow. My GitHub login never enters the sandbox.

Clearsky itself only reads. It never replies, merges or marks anything as read.

The chat is useful. The list is what I would keep if I had to choose.
path: What an agent needs to know, I needed too

items.title: Where nobody has looked yet
items.text:
I do not like software that tracks where people are. I have started on an app that does exactly that.

The idea came after a search for a missing person near where I grew up.

In a search, many people walk for many hours. Most of them are volunteers. They are sent out in directions, they come back and they are sent out again. What nobody has in the end is a picture of where they actually walked.

That picture matters for what it does not show. Ground that has been walked ten times does not need an eleventh. What you want to know is where nobody has been. The cold spots.

So the idea is simple. An app on the phone logs where you walk. Everyone in the same search shares a project, and the tracks become a heat map. The places with no heat are where to look closer. It would work for a person, a car or a boat.

A sketch of the idea. Shaded squares have been walked, darker for more passes. Nobody has been here. This is where to look closer.

items.title: The part I do not like
items.text:
It is a location tracker. It records where a person is, every few seconds, and sends it to a server. That is the kind of data I argue against collecting in every other setting.

So how do you build that without becoming what you dislike?

My answer so far is that nothing happens by itself. You join one search by scanning a barcode, and by scanning it you agree to share your location with that search. There is no account that follows you around. The tracking belongs to that project and has no reason to exist outside it.

Is that enough? I am not sure. A map of where volunteers walked is harmless in a search. The same data says where each of them was that night, and for how long. It should be coarse, and it should not live longer than the search does.

I have started on it. An Android app first, since that is what I know.

I hope it never gets used. I would still like it to exist.

items.title: Why I wrote my own date-time parser
items.text:
1488153600. Is that seconds or milliseconds? You find out when the date lands in 1970 or in the year 49,000. APIs send timestamps like that since a number is fast to parse. I wanted to see how much of that is real, so I wrote a parser this weekend.

It covers a very small part of date and time handling. I have not touched calendars or time zone rules. java.time does those, and does them well. What I wrote reads and writes one format, the one in RFC 3339:

2017-12-27T23:45:32Z
2017-12-27T23:45:32.999Z
2017-12-27T18:45:32.999999-05:00

That is the format an API should use for a timestamp. It has been a standard since 2002, and still many do not. There are endless APIs with their own date formats, and there are the ones that gave up and send epoch numbers.

I understand the epoch people, and they are who this is for. A number is fast to read. A formatted timestamp goes through a general pattern parser that can handle any format you give it, and you pay for that on every field of every message. So you get a number that nobody can read in a log.

So the argument for the unreadable format is speed. I wanted to see how much of that is real.

The parser in itu knows the format in advance. The year is in the first four characters and the month in the next two after the dash. There is no pattern to interpret, so it reads digits at fixed positions and checks them.

Timestamps parsed per second, in millions. Higher is better. java.time (Java 8) 0.55 java.util (Java 7) 0.74 Apache FastDateFormat 1.08 itu 15.6

Formatting went from about 2 million per second to 12.7 million.

I do not fully trust these numbers. It is a loop with a timer around it, on my machine, and I wrote both the parser and the test. The two older ones were also given a single hard-coded format, which is kinder to them than real use. But a factor of 28 over java.time does not come from measuring badly.

So the speed argument for epoch numbers is mostly an argument about one slow parser. With that gone, you can send a timestamp that a person can read.

The first rule of date and time handling is that you do not write your own, and I still agree with it. This is one format. java.time does the rest.
path: Why I wrote my own date-time parser

items.title: Why r7 moved from Undertow to Helidon Níma
items.text:
r7 now runs every request on a virtual thread of its own, the upstream call included. To get that I replaced the HTTP server under it, five months in and a week and a half before the first beta.

r7 started on Undertow. It is a good server. I had no bug to point at, and no number that forced the move.

What I had was an execution model I liked better. In Helidon Níma every request runs on a virtual thread of its own, the upstream call included. The code for a request reads from top to bottom: read the request, run the filters, call the upstream, write the response. It blocks where it waits, and that is fine, since a blocked virtual thread costs almost nothing.

There are no worker pools to size and no handoff between an I/O thread and a worker. There is also no reactive chain. I have written a gateway on a reactive stack before, and a stack trace from it tells you very little about what your code was doing. Debugging it is a pain in the neck.

For a gateway that people extend with their own filters, that matters more than a few percent. A filter is plain Java that runs on the request's thread. If it blocks, it blocks that request and nothing else.
path: Why r7 moved from Undertow to Helidon Níma

items.title: What it took
items.text:
Less than I feared, and the reason is boring. The request guards and the tests had already been made server-neutral, so the end-to-end suite could run against both servers. When it was green on Helidon, Undertow went out, with its own settings: the read timeout, the proxy client and the "advanced" block.

Swapping the server this late is something I would question in a review. But it was before the first beta, with nobody depending on the old settings, and that door closes on release day.
path: Why r7 moved from Undertow to Helidon Níma

items.title: My first RFID application shipped! (6 April 2005)
items.text:
As I started out as an intern in an RFID company, I started out by playing around with their development kit. As I found this interesting, I started to develop a little RFID tag editor. This program was actually just meant to be for fun, but when my boss saw it, he wanted to include it in the development kit as an example application!

This was of course cool, but I felt that I needed to clean up the code and make some improvements to it before it could be released. After some final testing I think that it is stable enough, although not feature-rich enough. The RFID jungle is huge, and I would like to improve features like the tag manufacturer recognition and tag size/page size attributes. Well, there might perhaps be a later version at a later time...

Now it will be shipped in the package, and this means that it already has been sent to Spain, the U.S. and the Arab Emirates!
